title: lock, Interlocked and deadlock
sub: How to fix races without hanging the program
cards/0/body: lock (obj) { … } lets only one thread into the block. The others wait at the door until it leaves.
cards/0/deep: lock is Monitor.Enter/Exit inside try/finally. Since .NET 9 and C# 13 there's a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type, and lock on it is more efficient. Don't do lock(this) or lock on a string: other code can reach those objects and take the same lock.
cards/1/task: Same count++, but inside a lock. Try to get 1 again, then run both threads to completion.
cards/2/q: Why couldn't you lose an increment with lock?
cards/2/options/0: While A is inside the lock, B can't start its steps
cards/2/options/2: lock runs threads one after another from the start of the program
cards/2/explain: Inside the lock, the read, add and write run as one chunk relative to other threads using the same lock.
cards/3/body: For simple number operations there's Interlocked: Increment, Add, Exchange, CompareExchange. The CPU runs them as a single indivisible instruction, faster than a lock.
cards/4/task: Interlocked.Increment: run 2 threads × 1,000 and check the result.
cards/5/q: What do 2 threads × 1,000 calls to Interlocked.Increment give you?
cards/5/options/1: A different number around 2,000 each time
cards/5/explain: Read, add and write are one indivisible operation. You can't lose an increment.
cards/6/body:
If a thread needs two locks and another thread takes the same locks in the opposite order, they can get stuck forever: each waits for the lock the other holds.

That's a deadlock. The program doesn't crash. It just hangs.
cards/7/task: A takes L1, then L2. B does the opposite. Drive the threads into a deadlock.
cards/8/task: Fix it: make both threads take the locks in the same order. Then run them to completion.
cards/9/q: What's the main rule against lock deadlocks?
cards/9/options/0: Always take locks in the same order
cards/9/options/1: Take as many locks at once as you can
cards/9/explain: With a single order, the second thread waits on the first lock and can't grab the second one. No waiting cycle forms.
cards/10/pairs/0/1: One thread in the block, the rest wait
cards/10/pairs/1/1: An indivisible operation on a number
cards/10/pairs/2/1: Threads wait for each other forever
cards/10/pairs/3/1: The result depends on thread switches
